name: Elite

lesson.text: Welcome to Stage 1: Elite! A decimal is a number with a whole part and a fractional part, separated by a decimal point.
Each place after the point is ten times smaller than the one before it.
To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points first. Add a zero if it helps!
To multiply, ignore the point, multiply, then put the point back. Count the decimal places in the problem.

facts: The dot in a decimal number is called the decimal point.
Digits after the decimal point show values smaller than one.
The first place after the point is tenths: 0.3 means 3 tenths.
The second place after the point is hundredths: 0.07 means 7 hundredths.
The third place after the point is thousandths: 0.005 means 5 thousandths.
Adding zeros at the end does not change a decimal: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500.
Compare decimals place by place from the left: 0.7 is greater than 0.65 because 7 tenths beats 6 tenths.
Always line up the decimal points when you add or subtract.
To round to the nearest tenth, look at the hundredths digit. If it is 5 or more, round up.
When multiplying, count the decimal places in the problem. The answer has the same number.
Multiplying by 10 moves the point one place right: 3.6 × 10 = 36.
Dividing by 10 moves the point one place left: 3.6 ÷ 10 = 0.36.
When dividing a decimal by a whole number, the point in the answer goes straight above the point in the problem.
We read 7.5 as “seven and five tenths”. The word “and” marks the point.
Whole numbers have a hidden decimal point at the end: 5 = 5.0.
We read 0.25 as “twenty-five hundredths”.
Money uses decimals: 12.75 pesos is 12 pesos and 75 centavos.
To subtract 6.35 from 10, write 10 as 10.00 first.
Multiplying by 100 moves the point two places right: 0.45 × 100 = 45.
Dividing by 100 moves the point two places left: 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45.
